questions.q: What is typically true about how teams set up the Test and Production workspaces for a pipeline?
options: They're usually created fresh, specifically for the pipeline, starting with nothing but what the pipeline deploys
They reuse the exact same workspace as Development
They must be created by Microsoft support
They can never be assigned a workspace at all
questions.explain: While Development often points at an existing, actively-worked-in workspace, Test and Production are typically fresh workspaces created specifically for the pipeline.

questions.q: What does a fully connected pipeline canvas show, compared to a brand-new, unassigned one?
options: A list of every tenant admin
Real content, refresh times, and deployment status for each stage, instead of empty placeholder cards
Only the names of the three stages, with no other detail ever
Nothing changes — it always looks the same
questions.explain: Once workspaces are assigned, the stages show real items, refresh times, and whether the last deployment succeeded — useful for a reviewer checking whether Production is current.

questions.q: What does an 'Only in source' status mean when comparing two pipeline stages?
options: The item has been deleted from both stages
The item exists in the source stage but hasn't been deployed to the destination stage yet
The item is broken and cannot be deployed under any circumstances
The item is identical in both stages
questions.explain: 'Only in source' flags an item present in the source stage (like Development) that hasn't made it to the destination stage (like Test) yet — something a reviewer should notice before approving a deployment.

questions.q: What does the deploy confirmation dialog show before a deployment actually happens?
options: Exactly which items are different and which are new, plus an option to continue even if one item fails
Nothing — deployments happen instantly with no preview
A list of every user who has ever accessed the workspace
Only the total file size being transferred
questions.explain: The deploy dialog lists the items that are different or new as part of the deployment, and includes a checkbox letting the deployment continue even if one or more items fail.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why might a team leave the 'continue deployment if items fail' checkbox unchecked for a batch containing a certified dataset?
options: Because the checkbox doesn't actually do anything
Because checking it always deletes the entire workspace
Because certified datasets can never be deployed through a pipeline
So one failed item can't silently slip through alongside the rest of a deployment involving high-trust content
questions.explain: Leaving it unchecked means a single failure stops the whole deployment, which is a deliberate safeguard for higher-stakes batches rather than letting a broken item through alongside successful ones.
